newsitem.title: JAPAN: Toyota Motor gets back on feet after fire.
newsitem.headline: Toyota Motor gets back on feet after fire.

text.p: Toyota Motor Corp has managed to get its domestic production back on track after a shutdown caused by a fire at a brake parts supplier.
But the two-day closure shows that a much-vaunted inventory system designed to reduce costs carries its risks, industry analysts said on Friday.
The revolutionary "kanban" inventory system, known as just-in-time, was introduced in Japan in 1963 and is now standard practice for all kinds of manufacturers around the world.
It allows companies to reduce costs by keeping a bare minimum of supplies on hand and instead receive frequent deliveries from suppliers.
But it all went wrong last Saturday when a fire at Aisin Seiki Co Ltd's Kariya plant in Aichi Prefecture stopped the delivery of all brake parts supplied to Toyota.
The impact was felt almost immediately. By Tuesday, Japan's largest carmaker had shut all of its domestic plants. Normal production is not expected until Monday, a Toyota spokesman told Reuters.
"After getting back to normal, we will start investigating our current parts sourcing practices to avoid a similar accident in the future," the Toyota spokesman said.

Seiji Sugiura, an auto analyst at Nomura Research Institute, said the accident would prompt Toyota to make sure it had more than one source for the brake components, a practice already followed for other key parts.
Toyota said it has no plans to revise the "just in time" system.
"The important thing is to quickly tide yourself over during a crisis, not hold excess inventories which raise production costs," the Toyota spokesman said.
Industry groups agreed that the just-in-time system is here to stay,

"When you have the kanban system, production cuts may be unavoidable in some cases. But no Japanese makers would increase their inventories and eliminate kanban," said Yoshifumi Tsuji, chairman of the Japan Automobile Manufacturers Association.
The effects of the fire spread well beyond Aisin Seiki and Toyota.
The government's Economic Planning Agency said every day of Toyota's shutdown lopped 0.1 percent off February's industrial output.
